Plain text is your original summary, kept word-for-word. Coloured boxes are genuine 7th-edition additions/revisions; red marks important cautions. Figures & Tables sit in the right margin (zoom to read the book caption). Chapter 5's figure numbers are unchanged from your summary.
Terminology & Developmental Stages
  • Deformity: a tissue that initially formed normally and then failed to continue normal development.
  • Malformation: a tissues that did not form normally from the beginning.
  • Occasionally, a specific cause of a dentofacial problem is apparent (as in mandibular deficiency secondary to a childhood fracture of the jaw "a deformity"), or the characteristic malocclusion that accompanies some genetic syndromes, which would be "a malformation".
  • Embryonic stage (3rd-8th week), Fetal stage (9th week-birth)
Expanded terminology (7th) The 7th edition frames this through dysmorphology (pioneered by geneticist David W. Smith in the 1960s): a malformation is a congenital anomaly due to altered primary development, whereas a deformation is an altered shape/position from mechanical forces. It also lists three prenatal stages — germinal (0–2 wk), embryonic (3–8 wk), fetal (9 wk–birth); germinal-period problems are largely failure of implantation (~60% of natural conceptions).
Specific Causes of Malocclusion

I Disturbances in "Embryonic" Development ("Embryogenesis" 3rd to 8th week of prenatal development)

  • Chemical and other agents capable of producing embryologic defects if given at the critical time are called teratogens. Table 5.1
  • Facial form changes are particularly dramatic over approximately 1-month period, which is between the end of the fourth week and the end of embryogenesis (eighth week)".
  • Genetic and environmental insults (means anything that could have an adverse impact on normal development) can affect the developing face and jaws throughout the embryonic period.
  • Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS; Fig 5.3) (3rd week)
    • A phenotype that arises in the third week of development
    • Typically caused by exposure to very high maternal ethanol levels.
    • The resulting facial deformity and developmental delay occur frequently enough to be implicated in many cases of midface deficiency. The delay in dental development matches the skeletal delay.
  • Neural crest cells:
    • Many craniofacial defects are related to neural crest cell abnormalities, including cell death and migration errors.
    • Neural crest cell migration away from the cranial neural folds occurs in the latter part of the third and the early part of the fourth week "before the mother knows she is pregnant" Fig 5.4 and this is a time of particular vulnerability to teratogens.
    • Neural crest cells make up practically all of the mesenchyme of the face and differentiate into much of its skeletal and connective tissue, including the bones of the jaw and the teeth.
    • Also, neural crest cells play a major role in formation of the heart and great vessels. This is the basis for the common co-occurrence of craniofacial abnormalities and heart defects.
    • Neural crest defects can be drug-induced, or genetic alterations "as in Treacher Collins syndrome".
  • Treacher Collins syndrome: (Fig 5.5) (4th week)
    • Characterized by reduced levels of mesenchymal tissue, especially in the lateral aspects of the face.
    • known to be due to mutations in the TCOF1 gene.
    • Malformations very similar to this syndrome may result from teratogenic effects on embryos at stages present in the fourth week. (Accutane, Thalidomide, Valium)
Updated genes (7th) The 7th edition lists Treacher Collins as due to mutations in TCOF1, POLR1C and POLR1D (your summary, from the 6th, gives TCOF1 only).
  • Craniofacial Microsomia (Fig 5.6) (4th week)
    • Often called (hemifacial microsomia) also is characterized by deficient development in lateral facial areas.
    • Typically, the external ear is deformed and both the ramus of the mandible and associated soft tissues (muscle, fascia) are deficient or missing.
    • Facial asymmetry is always seen, and cranial as well as facial structures are affected.
    • The major cause is insult to cell populations (including neural crest cells). (Accutane, Thalidomide, Valium)
New subsection (7th) The 7th adds microtia — malformation of the external ear (middle/internal ear components can be affected too). It is multifactorial (syndromes, gene mutations, environmental factors); most commonly it occurs with hemifacial microsomia.
  • Cleft Lip and/or Palate (Figs 5.8, 9, 10) (7th week / 9-10th week)
    • The most common congenital defects involving the face and jaws.
    • In embryo, the premaxillary segment gives rise to:
      • The philtral part of the upper lip
      • The portion of the alveolar ridge that contains the upper central incisors and the medial portions of the upper lateral incisors.
    • The lateral component of each of the upper lateral incisors appears to be of maxillary tissue origin.
    • Primary palate "pre-maxilla" includes that portion of the alveolar ridge containing four incisors.
    • Secondary palate forms the remaining hard palate and all soft palate.
    • In cleft lip, failure of union of the (lateral nasal prominence and maxillary) with (the premaxillary segment) occurs Fig 5.8C
    • Lip clefts may be unilateral, bilateral, complete, or incomplete Fig 5.9.
    • In cleft palate, failure of union of the (Palatine shelves "secondary palate") occurs
    • For the lip, closure is normally completed by the seventh week, and for the secondary palate, union occurs early in the fetal period of development (weeks 9 and 10). Fig 5.10
    • About 60% of individuals with a cleft lip also have a cleft palate. This may be a result of:
      • A concurrent tissue abnormality in the lip or primary palate and the secondary palate tissue
      • Or, excessive facial width that follows the lip clefting and places the secondary palatal shelves too far apart to unite in the midline.
    • A number of possible causes of cleft lip and palate have been identified, including exposure to some teratogens. maternal smoking is a definite risk factor.
    • In addition to "typical" cleft lip and cleft palate, unusual facial clefts occur that also result from the failure of facial prominences to properly form or unite. Examples include macrostomia, a defect at the junction of the maxillary and mandibular prominences
New epidemiology (7th) Orofacial clefts are the most common congenital defects outside chromosomal defects — second only to heart defects. About 30% are syndromic (70% unknown origin); roughly 1 in 700 babies is born with a cleft palate and 1 in 1600 with a cleft lip and palate (US).
  • Craniosynostosis syndromes:
    • Major group of craniofacial malformations, involve developmental abnormalities in the fetal period.
    • Result from abnormally early closure of the sutures between specific bones of the craniofacial complex and can be caused by a variety of mutations involving fibroblast growth factor receptor genes.
    • Surgical release of the prematurely fused areas is needed to maintain normal head shape and facial proportions. The ideal time for surgery is (with a few exceptions) between 6 and 9 months of age.
    • Crouzon's syndrome (Fig 5.11) is the most frequently occurring member of the group of synostosis syndromes that affect the face.
    • Caused by prenatal fusion of the superior and posterior sutures of the maxilla along the wall of the orbit.
    • The premature fusion frequently extends posteriorly into the cranium, producing distortions of the cranial vault as well.
    • The fusion in the orbital area prevents the maxilla from translating downward and forward, and the result is severe underdevelopment of the middle third of the face.
    • Surgery to release the sutures coupled with distraction osteogenesis to advance the orbits often is necessary.
Updated (7th) The 7th gives suture-release surgery as ideal between 3 and 9 months (your summary, from the 6th, says 6 and 9 months), and adds helmet therapy to help reshape the head.
New detail (7th) Craniosynostosis incidence is 1/2200 births, 25% syndromic, with mutations in FGFR2, FGFR3, FGFR1, and TWIST1. Crouzon midface hypoplasia carries an increased risk of sleep-disordered breathing / obstructive sleep apnea.

II Growth Disturbances in the "Fetal and Perinatal Period"

  • Intrauterine molding:
    • Pressure against the developing face prenatally can lead to distortion of rapidly growing areas.
    • On rare occasions, an arm is pressed across the face in utero, resulting in severe maxillary deficiency at birth Fig 5.12.
    • Pierre Robin sequence:
      • A fetus' head is flexed tightly against the chest in utero, preventing the mandible from growing forward normally. The result is an extremely small mandible at birth, usually accompanied by a cleft palate because the restriction on displacement of the mandible forces the tongue upward and prevents normal closure of the palatal shelves.
      • It is not a syndrome that has a defined cause; instead, multiple causes can lead to the same sequence of events that produce the deformity.
      • The reduced volume of the oral cavity can lead to respiratory difficulty at birth, and it may be necessary to perform a tracheostomy so the infant can breathe.
      • Early mandibular advancement via distraction osteogenesis has been used recently in these severely affected infants to bring the tongue forward and provide more space for an airway so that the tracheostomy can be closed.
      • There is the possibility of normal growth thereafter and perhaps eventually a complete recovery. Some children with Pierre Robin sequence at birth do have favorable mandibular growth in childhood, but a smaller than normal mandible typically persists Fig 5.13, and catch-up growth during adolescence does not occur.
      • It has been estimated that about one-third of Pierre Robin patients have a defect in cartilage formation and can be said to have Stickler syndrome. Not surprisingly, this group has limited growth potential.
Updated (7th) The 7th states about 60% of Pierre Robin sequence is associated with a syndrome, the most common being Stickler (your summary, from the 6th, says about one-third have a cartilage defect / Stickler).
  • Birth Trauma to the Mandible:
    • In some difficult births, however, the use of forceps to the head to assist in delivery might damage either or both of the temporomandibular (TM) joints.
    • In light of the contemporary understanding that the condylar cartilage is not critical for proper growth of the mandible, it is not as easy to blame underdevelopment of the mandible on birth injuries. Children with deformities involving the mandible are much more likely to have a congenital syndrome.
New in 7th On birth trauma the 7th adds that the facial nerve (CN VII) is the most common cranial nerve injury, and that a tongue-lip adhesion is another surgical option to open the oropharyngeal airway in Pierre Robin sequence.

III Progressive Deformities in "Childhood"

  • Childhood Fractures of the Jaws
    • The condylar neck of the mandible is particularly vulnerable, and fractures of this area are relatively common in children. Fortunately, the condylar process tends to regenerate well after early fractures (75% of children with early fractures of the mandibular condylar process have normal mandibular growth afterward)
    • When a problem does arise following condylar fracture, it usually is asymmetric growth deficiency, with the injured side (or, in bilateral fractures, the more severely injured side) lagging behind Fig 5.14.
    • After such an injury, there is enough scarring around the TM joint that restrict translation of the condyle.
    • The best therapy, therefore, is conservative management at the time of injury and early mobilization of the jaw to minimize any restriction on movement. If deficient growth is observed, however, early treatment is needed (Growth Modification). (there would be little if any advantage from surgical open reduction of a condylar fracture in a child. the additional scarring produced by surgery could make things worse)
    • Rheumatoid arthritis (Fig 5.15), or a congenital absence of tissue as in craniofacial microsomia also can produce asymmetric mandibular deficiency.
Updated number (7th) The 7th edition (citing the best human data) raises this to about 80% to 85% of children with early condylar-process fractures having normal subsequent growth (your summary, from the 6th, says 75%).
  • Muscle Dysfunction
    • The facial muscles can affect jaw growth in two ways:
      1. The formation of bone at the point of muscle attachments depends on the activity of the muscle
      2. The musculature growth normally carries the jaws downward and forward.
    • Loss of part of the musculature is most likely to result from damage to the motor nerve (muscle atrophies). The result would be underdevelopment of that part of the face, with a deficiency of both soft and hard tissues Fig 5.16.
    • Excessive muscle contraction can restrict growth in much the same way as scarring after an injury. This effect is seen most clearly in torticollis, a twisting of the head caused by excessive tonic contraction of the neck muscles on one side Fig 5.17. The result is a facial asymmetry because of growth restriction on the affected side, which can be quite severe unless the contracted neck muscles are surgically detached at an early age.
    • Conversely, a major decrease in tonic muscle activity (as in muscular dystrophy, some forms of cerebral palsy, and various muscle weakness syndromes) allows the mandible to drop downward away from the rest of the facial skeleton. The result is increased anterior face height, distortion of facial proportions and mandibular form, excessive eruption of the posterior teeth, narrowing of the maxillary arch, and anterior open bite Fig 5.18.
New in 7th The 7th adds that less severe torticollis, if caught early, can be treated with Botox injections, neck braces, and/or physical therapy (rather than only surgical detachment).

IV Disturbances Arising in "Adolescence or Early Adult Life"

  • Hemimandibular hypertrophy (Formerly called Condylar Hyperplasia) (Fig 5.19)
    • Unilateral excessive growth of the mandible occurs in individuals who seem metabolically normal. Unknown etiology.
    • The excessive growth may stop spontaneously, but in severe cases removal of the affected condyle and reconstruction of the area are necessary.
  • Acromegaly
    • Caused by an anterior pituitary tumor that secretes excessive amounts of growth hormone, excessive growth of the mandible may occur, creating a skeletal Class III malocclusion in adult life Fig 5.20.
    • Often, mandibular growth accelerates again to the levels seen in the adolescent growth spurt, years after adolescent growth was completed.
    • Orthognathic surgery is likely to be necessary.

V Disturbances of Dental Development

  • Congenitally missing teeth
    • A genetic basis has been established for most instances of congenitally missing teeth (more formally called tooth agenesis), and some form of tooth agenesis appears as a phenotype in more than 150 syndromes.
    • Congenital absence of teeth results from disturbances during the initial stages of formation of a tooth: initiation and proliferation.
    • Anodontia, the total absence of teeth, is the extreme form. Oligodontia refers to congenital absence of many but not all teeth, whereas hypodontia implies the absence of only a few teeth.
    • Because the primary tooth buds give rise to the permanent tooth buds, there will be no permanent tooth if its primary predecessor was missing. (It is possible, however, for the primary teeth to be present and for some or all the permanent teeth to be absent.)
    • Anodontia and oligodontia are usually associated with ectodermal dysplasia, which has a genetic basis.
    • Individuals with ectodermal dysplasia have thin, sparse hair and an absence of sweat glands in addition to their characteristically missing teeth Fig 5.21.
    • Hypodontia is a relatively common finding. It appears that a polygenic multifactorial model of etiology is the best explanation of the cause.
    • As a general rule, if only one or a few teeth are missing, the absent tooth will be the most distal tooth of any given type (If a molar tooth is congenitally missing, it is third molar; if an incisor it is lateral; if a premolar it is the second. Rarely is a canine the only missing tooth.
Updated definition (7th) The 7th defines oligodontia as congenital absence of greater than six, but not all teeth (your summary, from the 6th, says "many but not all").
  • Malformed and Supernumerary teeth
    • Abnormalities in tooth size and shape result from disturbances during the morphodifferentiation stage of development, perhaps with some carryover from the histodifferentiation stage.
    • The most common abnormality is a variation in size, particularly of maxillary lateral incisors and mandibular or maxillary second premolars.
    • About 5% of the total population have a significant "tooth size discrepancy" (Bolton discrepancy)
    • Supernumerary teeth also result from disturbances during the initiation and proliferation stages of dental development can occur as part of a larger disease process or syndrome "cleidocranial dysplasia" or as an idiopathic finding.
    • The most common supernumerary tooth appears in the maxillary midline "mesiodens".
    • The presence of an extra tooth has great potential to disrupt normal occlusal development, and early intervention to remove it is usually required.
  • Traumatic displacement of teeth
    • When trauma to a primary tooth displaces the permanent tooth bud, there're two possible results:
      1. If the trauma occurs while the crown of the permanent tooth is forming, enamel formation will be disturbed and there will be a defect in the crown of the permanent tooth.
      2. If the trauma occurs after the crown is complete, the crown may be displaced relative to the root. Root formation may stop, leaving a permanently shortened root. More frequently, root dilaceration occur. Fig 5.24
    • If dilaceration is severe enough, and might require the root to extend out through the alveolar bone, it may be necessary to extract the tooth.
    • Teeth that were displaced laterally by trauma usually should be repositioned as early as possible. Immediately after the accident, an intact tooth usually can be moved back to its original position rapidly and easily. After healing (which takes 2 to 3 weeks), orthodontics or surgery may be necessary to reposition the tooth, and ankylosis may make this impossible.
Updated (7th) For a laterally displaced tooth with no occlusal interference, the 7th delays repositioning to orthodontics at a minimum of 3 months after healing (your summary, from the 6th, says healing takes 2–3 weeks), and adds partial root amputation as an option.
Genetic Influences
  • Certain types of malocclusion run in families. The Hapsburg jaw, the prognathic mandible of this European royal family, is the best known example
  • For much of the 20th century, thoughts about how malocclusion could be produced by inherited characteristics focused on two major possibilities:
    • The first would be an inherited disproportion between the size of the teeth and the size of the jaws, which would produce crowding or spacing.
    • The second would be an inherited disproportion between the size and/or shape of the upper and lower jaws, which would cause improper occlusal relationships.
  • If malocclusion or a tendency to malocclusion is inherited, the mechanism is not the independent inheritance of discrete morphologic characteristics such as tooth and jaw sizes.
  • Achondroplasia (an autosomal dominant trait) is rare in humans Fig 5.27. In addition to short limbs, the cranial base does not lengthen normally because of the deficient growth at the synchondroses, the maxilla is not translated forward to the normal extent, and a relative midface deficiency occurs.
  • Harris and Johnson concluded that the heritability of craniofacial (skeletal) characteristics was relatively high but that of dental (occlusal) characteristics was low.
  • In a recent study in Brazil, the investigators concluded that there is a major gene that influences the expression of mandibular prognathism. This does not mean that a single gene is responsible. It is apparent that what we call Class III malocclusion, or even the subcategory mandibular prognathism, really is a group of different phenotypes.
  • In general, similar malocclusions are likely to be seen in siblings, especially if the malocclusion is severe, perhaps because their genetically influenced facial types and growth patterns lead to similar responses to environmental factors.
  • The long-face pattern of facial deformity seems to be the second most likely type of deformity to run in families.
  • The extent to which other types of malocclusion are related to genetic influences is less clear.
Environmental Influences

I Equilibrium Consideration

  • A key consideration is that the supporting structures of the dentition (PDL and alveolar bone) are constructed to withstand heavy forces of short duration such as those from mastication.
  • During mastication, the fluid in the PDL space acts as a shock absorber, so that the soft tissues in the PDL are not compressed, although bending of alveolar bone occurs.
  • Only if pressure is maintained long enough to squeeze out the fluid (a few seconds) is there an impact on the soft tissues.
  • Only light force of long duration (6 hours or so per day) is important in determining whether there is enough of an imbalance of forces to lead to tooth movement. Means that if the balance between long-duration pressure from the tongue vs lip or cheek pressure changes, tooth movement would be expected.
  • If an injury to the soft tissue of the lip results in scarring and contracture, the adjacent incisors will be moved lingually as the lip tightens against them Fig 5.28. On the other hand, if restraining pressure by the lip or cheek is removed, the teeth move outward in response to unopposed pressure from the tongue Fig 5.29A.
  • It seems unlikely, however, that the intermittent short-duration pressures created when the tongue and lips contact the teeth during swallowing or speaking would have any significant impact on tooth position.
  • As with masticatory forces, the pressure magnitudes would be great enough to move a tooth, but the duration is inadequate Table 5.2.
  • Equilibrium considerations also apply to the skeleton, including the facial skeleton. Skeletal alterations occur all the time in response to functional demands.

II Masticatory Function

  • The pressures generated by chewing activity potentially could affect dentofacial development in two ways:
    • Greater use of the jaws, with higher and/or more prolonged biting force, could increase the dimensions of the jaws and dental arches
    • Less use of the jaws might lead to underdeveloped dental arches and crowded and irregular teeth.
  • Function and Dental Arch Size
    • The size and shape of the muscular processes of the jaws reflect muscle size and activity. Fig 5.30
    • In contrast, the heavy intermittent forces produced during mastication should have little direct effect on tooth position, so the size of the dental arches would be affected by function only if their bony bases were widened.
    • During the development, vertical jaw relationships clearly are affected by muscular activity
    • Is it possible that a preadolescent child's masticatory effort plays a major role in determining dental arch dimensions? that seems unlikely, but the precise relationship remains unknown.
  • Biting Force and Eruption
    • It was noted some years ago that short-face individuals have higher and long-face persons lower maximum biting forces than those with normal vertical dimensions. Fig 5.31
    • It seems more likely that the different biting force is an effect rather than a cause.
    • Findings suggest that the force exerted by the masticatory muscles is not a major environmental factor in controlling tooth eruption and not an etiologic factor for most patients with deep bite or open bite. In the absence of syndromes, there is no reason to believe that how a patient bites is a major determinant of either dental arch size or vertical dimensions.

III Sucking and Other Habits

  • Almost all normal children engage in non-nutritive sucking of a thumb or pacifier
  • As a general rule, sucking habits during the primary dentition years have little if any long-term effect. If these habits persist beyond the time that the permanent teeth begin to erupt, however, malocclusion characterized by flared and spaced maxillary incisors, lingually positioned lower incisors, anterior open bite, and a narrow upper arch is the likely result
  • The characteristic malocclusion associated with sucking arises from a combination of direct pressure on the teeth and an alteration in the pattern of resting cheek and lip pressures. When a thumb or finger is placed between the anterior teeth:
    • The mandible must be positioned downward to accommodate it.
    • The interposed thumb directly impedes incisor eruption.
    • The separation of the jaws alters the vertical equilibrium on the posterior teeth, and as a result, there is more eruption of posterior teeth (1 mm of elongation posteriorly opens the bite about 2 mm anteriorly, so this can be a powerful contributor to the development of anterior open bite Fig 5.35.)
    • The tongue must be lowered, which decreases pressure by the tongue against the lingual of upper posterior teeth. At the same time, cheek pressure against these teeth is increased as the buccinator muscle contracts during sucking (result in constricted maxilla) Fig 5.36. (Cheek pressures are greatest at the corners of the mouth, and this probably explains why the maxillary arch tends to become V-shaped, with more constriction across the canines than the molars)
  • Mild displacement of the primary incisor teeth is often noted in a 3 or 4 year old thumb-sucker, but if sucking stops at this stage, normal lip and cheek pressures soon restore the teeth to their usual positions. If the habit persists after the permanent incisors have begun to erupt, orthodontic treatment may be necessary to overcome the resulting tooth displacements.
  • Transverse constriction of the maxillary arch is the aspect of the malocclusion least likely to correct spontaneously. In many children with a history of thumb-sucking, if the maxillary arch is expanded transversely, both the incisor protrusion and anterior open bite will improve spontaneously.
  • Sucking habits often exceed the time threshold necessary to produce an effect on the teeth, but even prolonged sucking has little impact on the underlying form of the jaws.

IV Tongue Thrusting

  • "Tongue thrust swallowing" (Fig 5.37) still is often thought to be a cause of malocclusion despite the number of studies that have found no such relationship.
  • Laboratory studies have indicated that individuals who place the tongue tip forward when they swallow usually do not have more tongue force against the teeth than those who keep the tongue tip back; in fact, tongue pressure may be lower.
  • Swallowing is not a learned behavior but is integrated and controlled physiologically at subconscious levels, so whatever the pattern of swallow, it cannot be considered a habit in the usual sense.
  • The mature or adult swallow pattern appears in some normal children as early as age 3 but is not present in the majority until about age 6 and is never achieved in 10% to 15% of a typical population.
  • A tongue thrust swallow is a useful physiologic adaptation if you have an open bite, which is why an individual with an open bite usually also has a tongue thrust swallow.
  • After a sucking habit stops, the anterior open bite tends to close spontaneously, but the position of the tongue between the anterior teeth persists for a while as the open bite closes.
  • "Tongue thrusting" in young children is often a normal transitional stage in swallowing.
  • Tongue thrust swallowing is seen primarily in two circumstances:
    • Younger children with reasonably normal occlusion, in whom it represents only a transitional stage in normal physiologic maturation
    • Individuals of any age with displaced incisors (or open bite), in whom it is an adaptation to the space between the teeth.
  • A tongue thrust swallow therefore is more likely to be the result of displaced incisors, not the cause. It follows, of course, that correcting the tooth position should cause a change in swallow pattern, and this usually happens. It is neither necessary nor desirable to try to teach the patient to swallow differently before beginning orthodontic treatment.
  • Tongue thrust swallowing simply has too short a duration to have an impact on tooth position (1 second).
  • On the other hand, if a patient has a forward resting posture of the tongue, the duration of this light pressure could affect tooth position. In a child who has an open bite, tongue posture may be a factor, but the swallow itself is not.

V Respiratory pattern

  • To breathe through the mouth, one must lower the mandible and tongue and extend (tip back) the head. If these postural changes were maintained, three effects on growth would be expected:
    1. Anterior face height would increase, and posterior teeth would super-erupt
    2. Unless there was unusual vertical growth of the ramus, the mandible would rotate down and back, opening the bite anteriorly and increasing overjet
    3. Increased pressure from the stretched cheeks might cause a narrower maxillary dental arch.
  • Exactly this type of malocclusion often is associated with mouth breathing (note its similarity to the pattern also blamed on sucking habits and tongue thrust swallow) "adenoid facies" Fig 5.39.
  • It appears that research to this point on respiration has established two opposing principles, leaving a large gray area between them:
    • Total nasal obstruction (although rare compared to partial nasal constriction) is highly likely to alter the pattern of growth and lead to malocclusion in experimental animals and humans, and individuals with a high percentage of oral respiration are over-represented in the long-face population.
    • The majority long-face individuals have no evidence of nasal obstruction and must therefore have some other etiologic factor as the principal cause.
  • Mouth breathing, in short, may contribute to the development of orthodontic problems but is difficult to indict as a frequent etiologic agent.
New — airway & OSA (7th) The 7th adds a major airway section that reverses the old morphology link:
  • Systematic reviews/meta-analyses of children with sleep-study–diagnosed OSA have failed to find a strong relationship between facial morphology and the disease — SNB and mandibular-plane differences are only a few degrees, and smaller intermolar widths (~2 mm) have little clinical relevance. Most children with OSA appear within normal limits; OSA's etiology also involves obesity, age, and gender.
  • Orthodontics and the airway: a systematic review/meta-analysis found no strong evidence that premolar extractions reduce pharyngeal airway volume or minimal cross-sectional area. A large Minnesota study (~2800 four-premolar-extraction adults matched to full-dentition controls) found no difference — about 10% of both groups had OSA (the general-population rate).
Etiology in Contemporary Perspective
  • Edward Angle and his contemporaries, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, took for granted that malocclusion was a disease of civilization and blamed it on improper function of the jaws under the "degenerate" modern conditions.
  • Classic (mendelian) genetics developed rapidly in the first part of the 20th century, its view was that malocclusion is primarily the result of inherited dentofacial proportions, which might be altered somewhat by developmental variations.
  • As the 21st century moves ahead, a more balanced view seems to be emerging. The research has not yet clarified the precise role of heredity as an etiologic agent for malocclusion. The relatively high heritability of craniofacial dimensions and the relatively low heritability of dental arch variations now have been established, but exactly how this relates to the etiologic process of malocclusions that have both skeletal and dental components remains unknown.
  • Conclusions about the etiology of most orthodontic problems are difficult because several interacting factors probably played a role.
